details:
**Yad**
The small pointer, usually shaped like a rod ending in a hand with an extended index finger ("yad" means "hand"), used to follow the text while reading from a Torah scroll. It is used because the parchment should not be touched by bare hands, both to protect the scroll and to avoid making it impure.

**Simchat Torah**
The joyous holiday ("Rejoicing in the Torah") in the month of Tishrei that comes right after Sukkot, coinciding with or following Shemini Atzeret, the "eighth day of assembly." Torah scrolls are taken out of the Ark and carried in circuits while congregants sing and dance, sometimes in the street, as the annual cycle of readings ends and starts again.

**Aron kodesh (Torah Ark)**
The cabinet or chest in a synagogue in which the Torah scrolls are kept, usually on the wall facing Jerusalem. It is covered by a decorated curtain called the parochet, and the scrolls inside are often adorned with crowns.

**613 commandments (mitzvot)**
The traditional number of commandments contained in the Torah. The last of them, the 613th, commands every Jew to write (or have written) a Torah scroll.

**Sofer**
The trained scribe who handwrites a Torah scroll in a special script (ktav stam) with decorative crowns (tagin) on certain letters, using ink on parchment made of gevil or klaf. A scroll has 304,805 letters with no vowels, often 42 lines per column, and can take over a year to write; a sheet with errors must be replaced and a new one sewn in.

**Bar mitzvah**
The coming-of-age ceremony at which a Jewish boy, at age 13, is called up to read from the Torah for the first time. Girls do the same at a bat mitzvah in many communities.

**Parashot (weekly portions)**
The 54 sections into which the Torah is divided, one (or sometimes two) of which is read at synagogue each week so that the whole Torah is completed every year. The first portion, Bereshit ("In the Beginning"), covers the creation of the world.

**Bimah and aliyah**
The bimah is the raised platform in the synagogue on which the Torah scroll is laid and read. An aliyah ("going up," the same word used for immigrating to Israel) is the honor of being called to the bimah to recite the blessings over a Torah reading, which begin "Barchu et Adonai ha-mevorach," with the gabbai directing who is called; the final aliyah is called maftir.

**Cantillation (trope)**
The system of musical marks that indicate how each word of the Torah is to be chanted, including signs such as the etnachta, pazer, and the rare shalshelet, which appears only four times. Because the scroll itself has no vowels or trope marks, readers prepare with a printed guide called a tikkun.

**Hagbah and gelilah**
The rituals after a Torah reading in which the open scroll is lifted up to show the congregation (hagbah) and then rolled up and dressed in its cover (gelilah). During hagbah some congregants point toward the scroll with their little finger or the fringes of their prayer shawl.

**Tefillin and mezuzah**
Ritual objects containing small handwritten parchments with passages from the Torah, such as the Shema. Tefillin are small black leather boxes worn on the arm and head during weekday morning prayer, and a mezuzah is a case attached to a doorpost.

**Oral Torah**
The body of interpretation believed to have been given to Moses alongside the Written Torah and passed down orally until it was written down in the Mishnah and the Gemara, which together form the Talmud. It is rejected by the Karaites and was rejected by the ancient Sadducees, who accepted only the Written Torah.

**Five Books of Moses**
The Torah's contents: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, also called the Pentateuch and forming the first part of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh). Tradition holds that Moses wrote them, with Joshua writing the final lines describing Moses's death, and that Ezra the Scribe later restored and compiled the text.

**Documentary Hypothesis**
The scholarly theory that the Torah was assembled from several earlier independent sources, usually labeled J, E, D, and P, rather than written by a single author. It is a common modern-scholarship clue for the Torah.
